cards.text: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has been talking about money. He just said that when God gives a man riches and lets him enjoy them, that's a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 5:19). Now he says he's seen another evil under the sun, one that weighs heavily upon mankind.
Picture a man God gives riches, wealth and honor, so he lacks nothing his heart desires. The man's wish list is EMPTY, friend.

cards.question: This man has riches, wealth and honor, and he lacks nothing. So what's the evil the Teacher sees in it?

answers.text: God does not allow him to enjoy them
He loses all of it in one night
His honor slowly turns into shame

cards.question: God doesn't let the man enjoy his riches. Instead, a ___ will enjoy them.

cards.text: The Teacher calls it futile and a grievous affliction. That's like baking a perfect batch, and while you're still hunting for the oven mitts, some guy you've NEVER MET walks in and eats every single one.
Then the Teacher goes bigger: a man may father a hundred children and live for many years. A HUNDRED, friend, and my mustache was busy enough catching six of mine before they wobbled off the counter.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says a long life and a hundred children make up for a man being unsatisfied with his prosperity.
Say that man is unsatisfied with his prosperity and doesn't even receive a proper burial. Who does the Teacher say is better off than he is?

cards.text: The Teacher says the stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity. The child never sees the sun or knows anything.

cards.question: The stillborn child never sees the sun or knows anything. But what does the Teacher say that child has more of than the unsatisfied man?

cards.text: The Teacher says that holds even if the man lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. TWO THOUSAND YEARS, friend, and that's like sleeping the whole time and waking up STILL tired.

cards.question: True or false: after comparing that man and the stillborn child, the Teacher asks whether all go to the same place.

cards.text: Now the Teacher looks at every man's work. He says all a man's labor is for his mouth.

cards.question: The Teacher says all a man's labor is for his mouth. What does he say about that man's appetite?

answers.text: It is filled by hard work

cards.text: That's me with cookie dough: one batch and I'm DONE, then five minutes later I'm preheating the oven again. And now the Teacher starts asking hard questions.

cards.question: The Teacher starts asking hard questions. What does he ask about the wise man?

answers.text: What advantage he has over the fool
Why he keeps his wisdom hidden
Whether his name will last forever

cards.text: He also asks what gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others. Then he says what the eye can see is better than something else.

cards.question: The Teacher says what the eye can see is better than what?

cards.text: I think he means the batch on the cooling rack beats the ten you're daydreaming about. And the Teacher says this too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
Then he says whatever exists was named long ago, and it is known what man is.

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher says man can contend with one stronger than he.
Then the Teacher talks about words. He says the more words, the more ___.

cards.text: Then he asks how that profits anyone. Hoo, that one hit ME, friend, and I've been talking since the oven warmed up.

cards.question: The Teacher asks who knows what is good for a man during his life, which he passes through like a shadow. What does the Teacher say about the days of that life?
True or false: the Teacher says he can tell a man what will come after him under the sun.

findings.problem: The right answer 'They are few and fleeting' says the days are fleeting. In Ecclesiastes 6:12 the days are 'few', but 'fleeting' describes his life ('the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow'). The question also says 'like a shadow' just before it asks, which points the baker toward 'fleeting'.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: 'The more words, the more ___' asks the baker to finish the wording of a proverb-like line from Ecclesiastes 6:11. It does not test the movement or meaning of the passage.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card only restates Ecclesiastes 6:10a. It has none of Papa Dorin's voice and gives no context to help 'whatever exists was named long ago' make sense to the baker.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
